item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2020-07-15
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: There are a number of different methodologies when it comes to a naming scheme for elements in a project. It's good to stick to a standard and then have that standard be enforced across the project. If you are using a framework it's likely that you don't have much option when it comes to naming, but you could also start with a BEM style sheet for a smaller site and add on from there. This would require that you style most blocks to at least match the general style you want. You will get a lot of mileage out of scss/sass at that level." "" "Some of the problems that css frameworks CAN cause is that changing a variable can effect a lot of areas. " "" "Regardless, stick to a naming convention and use it, enforce it. Make it part of your eslinting if you can. Buy stickers. Give them to your developers. " "" "Suggesting naming conventions only work so long as they are easy to implement and understand. " "" "" "" "https://lnkd.in/esJnvzV

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2020-08-10
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Devs, using vs code and eslint with prettier/vetur. If you are having issues with the double linting or if you find yourself fighting with eslint, it COULD be because in your user settings file or somewhere in your chain you have turned on editor.formatonsave and it's formatting using a different subset of prettier than your eslint is running against." "" "In most cases the user settings will run after other stuff, or as is.aometimes the case, will run, then eslint will do it's thing, vetur does it's thing, then prettier wants to do it's thing... And then editor.formatonsave comes in and undoes some stuff you liked. " "" "Yup this is the life. item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: I LOVE using slots and scoped slots in components, reduce, reuse, recycle." "" "Reduce the amount of code you have to write: are you sick of writing that modal skeleton for the 1000th time? Yeah write a component that uses that skeleton and just set it up for slots, then you don't have to write that anymore" "" "Reuse the components you have to their full effect, add customization properties to them with defaults so that designers can override those styles when they need to, but they won't have to set up the "defaults"" "" "Recycle the code you have into better more readily reusable components. Don't write a data component that also handles how that specific component will look in a specific scenario, write that data component to render data back in a way that makes sense for it, but in such a way that it could be put on any page, any location. Keep the css scoped to that specific component and only it's interior." "" "" "Dang I think I'm passionate about #vuejs " " #learneveryday

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2020-09-02
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Some people are suggesting that remote work won't last or can't work because it's never worked in the past or because that's how we've always done thing." "" "The truth is most of us already have an unhealthy work/home life balance, how many of your current friends are co-workers?" " " "How many of your former friends were former colleagues and co-workers?" "" "How many of your significant others were from work outings or work related events?" "" "Kinda strange when you think about it, but even your best friend in school probably was only friends with you while you shared classes, schools etc." "" "We have had an obsession with identity, how many of us are defined by what we do during the work week. We plan our lives around work and it really should be the other way around. We work so that we can have an enjoyable life. Prior to this pandemic we used home as a vacation from work. Even I was guilty of that, people ask if I'm going to take a vacation I say, "I live in Florida, I'm always on vacation"." "" "Because of this pandemic I have been forced to rethink my own hobbies and activities, at the beginning of this I sat in front of my laptop almost 24/7. It sat in front of me on a TV tray by the couch, where I could work on a branch at a moment's notice. That's not healthy. #covıd19 #remoteemployees

item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: I'll be the first to admit I'm not the guy on the team that knows everything about one specific thing. I can't rant and rave about the ins and outs and reasons behind why the rest operator is different than a spread operator... (the developers just chuckled at that 3 dots)." "" "you see a rest operator and a spread operator visually.. are the same damn thing. " "" "...SOMETHING" "" "" "so in a reusable function component in react/Vue or whatever, you may have a a set of options that every reusable component uses but you don't want to have to make your function support each and every one. so your function arguments may look like:" "" "const mybutton = (title, text, ...otheroptions)=> {}" "" "in that scenario in my head I read it like:" "" "I send in title, I send in text... and all the rest" "" "now a spread operator visually does the same thing but it's how you use it:" "" "const newArray = [data, ...someotherarray];" "" "" "visually same thing. but very different applications. " "" "" "I can't tell you why they (ecma peeps) wrote it this way. I can't tell you how many big O notations it might be " "" "but I can use the damn thing just fine. " "" "" "so.. in closing do you want a lecture on the difference between a spread operator and a rest operator or do you just want me to code a dang thing for you and stop grading me on how they are different? " "" "seriously in my line of work it ain't the why.. it's the how. " "" "how you use it. how you apply it. " "" "I don't have a bachelor's degree in computer science. " "" "I have a bachelor's degree in web development and Interactive Media. " "" "aka I make the page I make it look good and functional and I usually work with other experts in their fields to do the other things. I'm not a miracle worker with c# you want that guy I recommend the dude at my last gig, he was a wiz. you need a cloud guy, I know a guy. last gig. wiz with that " "" "" "do I try and step on their toes? nah, but I am pretty dang good at my job, which is primarily full stack developer with an emphasis on front end and learning whatever new framework or tech is out there. " "" "you still want to use outdated angularjs? fine. I'll learn it but ill tell you how outdated it is (assuming you didn't mean you want me to use the latest angular... ya know that's different than the outdated version)" "" "you want me to integrate ai into my work flow.. fine done. " "" "you want me to completely learn a new testing suite (playwright) and single handedly convince an entire team to use it and write tests for it. fine. " "" "you need my skills, I need to trade my skills in for this piece of paper with dead presidents on it. could be monopoly money for all I care. item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-08-23
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Why I Think GitHub Copilot (and Tools Like It) Are Worth Trying:" "" "I heard about a manager who went so far as to fire developers who refused to at least try GitHub Copilot. At first, that struck me as pretty heavy-handed. But then I thought about it." "" "It took me less than three seconds to turn on Copilot (the free version) in VS Code. Granted, I already had a personal GitHub account not tied to a corporate SSO setup, so maybe there are some extra hoops in certain environments. Still, the barrier to entry is extremely low." "" "And that’s the point. He probably wasn’t demanding that everyone immediately restructure their entire workflow around AI. He just wanted people to flip the switch, experiment, and see how it could fit into their daily coding process. Adopt slowly. Work it in naturally." "" "For me, Copilot quickly solved one of my long-standing annoyances: remembering exact syntax. I’ve been writing code for years, but I still look up the shape of a basic for loop just to make sure I don’t miss a semicolon or misplace a variable. Normally, that means jumping to Google to search “JavaScript for loop example” or “Tailwind CSS 3-column responsive grid skeleton.”" "" "Now, I don’t need to leave my IDE." "" "Developers already tend to work with multiple monitors, but why dedicate an entire screen just for quick syntax lookups when the answers can live where you’re coding? That’s the same reason I’ve used GitLens for years. Instead of browsing through a repo to track down who changed a particular line, I can see it instantly in VS Code." "" "Copilot works the same way—it keeps you in flow. And staying in flow is where productivity really happens.

item.content:encoded: Attention new parents of December babies," "" "Let's rethink the notion of promising double presents for "birthmas." Growing up, I understood our financial situation and accepted receiving just one gift without any issue. However, constantly being reminded of our circumstances did not define my happiness. " "" "Now, as an adult, I've chosen to forego celebrating my birthday. Instead, I dedicate the day to my wife, exploring new experiences in Florida that bring her joy and excitement. Witnessing her delight in discovering something fresh and unfamiliar rejuvenates the occasion for me." "" "Reflecting on our move to Fort Myers in 2012, following a turbulent tornado season in 2011, Florida symbolized safety and a fresh start. Embracing new beginnings and creating lasting memories with loved ones transcends material gifts and fosters a deeper connection." "" "#NewPerspectives #CelebratingLove #MemorableExperiences

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-09-07
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: confession time. I, my dear reader, am a front end developer with ADHD and way too much curiosity about programming languages. I'll learn something just to learn it. I started coding html and css way back in 1999.. using notepad and an angelfire free website. I took known html examples from popular sites. pasted them into notepad, uploaded it using wsftp and just tinkered til I knew what a div was and meant. " "" "I learned php/MySQL at art institute of Pittsburgh online, but. see they didn't actually teach languages. we had to create a web page that accessed a db and pulled back a record to display. I chose php/MySQL because it seemed like the obvious choice, but I could have picked any language. just so long as it was a webpage that pulled a record from a db I've been a graphic designer at print shops, assisted in the creation of technical manuals for marine fuel polishing, migrated 2200 financial advisor websites from older in house CMS/sitecore 7 to sitecore 8, built an entirely new application in a new framework as a challenge from a boss. I learned react native just to provide support to a team of mobile application developers who just needed another react developer to slog through creating views in the app. " "" "and all of this.. yeah most of those things i did i learned as I went. but I already had a solid foundation to build up on. they didn't teach me how to code at art institute, they taught me how to learn and teach myself anything on the planet." "" "I got curious about golang... so I tinkered with it, I didn't know Vuejs at all when I picked it as the framework to write that new application in. The boss gave me requirements: must be fast. single page application, preferably some sort of JavaScript framework with a css framework that wouldn't require huge custom stylesheets. I worked with that to pick vuejs, using the buefy component library and Bulma css. I didn't know any of that stuff the Friday morning i came into the office and got the challenge. but the prototype was 75% finished by Friday evening, and 100% by Monday morning.. soooo who's the real winner? we got a rapid prototype off a vague but definable set of requirements. " "" "so . I guess the confession is, whether you hire me or not I'm not going to stop learning languages. better hop on board. " "" "I don't know why learning new things seems to be viewed as bad. he k I watch other people code in other languages just to see if I can apply any logic they use in solving a problem to something I'm doing. " "" "I can recognize patterns in code especially cross platform code (problem exists in c# layer but front end api works fine etc). I can trace through code faster than you drink your third cup of coffee in the morning and saunter around the office like the boss from office space. " "" "and better yet. I have a weird crazy brain for recalling random trivia... and how that relates is I'll remember some solution or bug we were talking about 6 months ago and where to find it in the code.." "" "#adhd

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-09-11
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: one day, I read something about the platform boot dot dev, I think I probably saw it on one of the many YouTube tutorials I watched while teaching myself how to use some new framework from watching someone else do it. " "" "it got me thinking, I loved playing world of Warcraft but sometimes the xp gap between levels could be insanely grindy.. you would be literally committing digital war crimes just to get 5xp..(cutting off troll ears and somehow finding out that not all trolls have ears, or not all fish have scales) but sure it at first felt like gambling like "awww come on surely that troll has two ears .. .. fuuuuuuuuu, come one just two more ears ..." " "" "what did it actually teach me? patience, and to set lower goals than just the end game, maybe it was "the next level", maybe it was "shoot everything is expensive, I don't even have 1 gold piece ..ok arathi highlands sucks for raw currency drops......but there's all these stone golems who drop these stupid grey items that I was just throwing on the ground.. I wonder how much one of those would sell for . just one .. oh?!.. what about 2?! fuuu... is it better to farm these than to try to find a mob willing to give 1gp per drop? I kinda think so .. so I lowered the bar, I'm going to farm these guys for 10 minutes and see how many greys I get and what it's worth is to that vendor over there .."" "" "point is, I was playing a game that already gamified my experience, but I wanted more, little tasks so I could feel like I was doing something important and accomplishing it, when all I wanted to do was curl up in bed and die. " "" "they say you are supposed to drink 64 ounces of water during some sort of period of time. why was I always convinced I needed to drink all 64oZ at once and if I didn't I failed? cuz I didn't understand how to gamify my life, and by extending that. my career. " "" "were you the kind of gamer who always wanted to know just a little more information, where the best loot was? did you use add-ons like auctioneer and advanced trade skill window? atlas loot? Titan panel? recount? dBm? " "" "you probably think that shit didn't matter. surprise, I give you an amazing man, who led a guild i was in, Josh Goldstein. I never would have figured that guild and raid leader experience in a stupid video game could translate. " "" "so maybe go slow. start with 1 oz, start with 1 silver piece, start with just listening to your guild leader, your raid leader. would you believe me if I opened with "guild leader and former raid leader works at random big name buzz worthy company? when I met Josh I didn't know anything about who he'd become, just he was this cool dude I met in wow.

item.content:encoded: gamer logic, applied to real life:" "" "" "" "ChatGPT" "You said:" "Hey Kyle. What does min/maxing mean? " "ChatGPT said:" "Alright James, here’s the breakdown—" "" "Min/maxing is a term from role-playing games (tabletop and video games) that stands for minimizing your weaknesses and maximizing your strengths." "" ""Min" → You put the minimum effort or points into things your character doesn’t really need." "" ""Max" → You put the maximum possible points into the stats, skills, or abilities that give you the biggest edge." "" "For example, in Dungeons & Dragons:" "" "If you want a powerhouse fighter, you might max Strength and Constitution (hit hard, survive long), while minimizing Intelligence and Charisma (because you don’t care if your character is dumb or ugly)." "" "A wizard might max Intelligence, and dump Strength to the bare minimum since they’re never swinging a sword." "" "It’s about optimization—squeezing every bit of effectiveness out of the rules, sometimes at the cost of making a character less balanced or less “realistic.”

item.content:encoded: Hedy Lamarr, born Hedwig Eva Maria Kiesler in Vienna, Austria, was an Austrian and American actress and inventor. She became a famous Hollywood actress, starring in films like Algiers (1938), Ziegfeld Girl (1941), and Samson and Delilah (1949). " "" "" "what a lot of people may not have known. was that she was an inventor as well. " "" "During World War II, Lamarr collaborated with composer George Antheil to invent a "Secret Communication System" that used frequency hopping technology. This invention was designed to prevent enemies from jamming radio-controlled torpedoes. While their invention was not used during the war, the technology became a precursor to modern-day technologies such as Wi-Fi, GPS, and Bluetooth. Her work was not widely recognized until late in her life, and she was posthumously inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2014. " "" "https://lnkd.in/ewvXf2gc" "

item.content:encoded: Samhain (pronounced SOW-in, with "sow" rhyming with "cow") is a Gaelic festival with ancient Celtic origins. It is a precursor to modern-day Halloween and holds deep historical and cultural significance." "Origins of Samhain" "A Celtic Festival: Samhain was a pagan religious festival celebrated by the ancient Celts, primarily in Ireland, Scotland, and the Isle of Man. It was one of the four major Gaelic fire festivals, marking a crucial point in the year." "The End of the Year: For the Celts, Samhain marked the end of the harvest season and the "lighter half" of the year, and the beginning of the "darker half," or winter. It was essentially the Celtic New Year's Eve." "The Veil Between Worlds: The most significant belief associated with Samhain was that the barrier between the human world and the spiritual "Otherworld" was at its thinnest. This allowed spirits—both benevolent ancestors and malevolent entities—to cross over. People would leave food and drink out for their ancestors to honor them, while wearing costumes and masks to disguise themselves from harmful spirits." "Bonfires and Rituals: Bonfires were a central part of the celebration. Community hearth fires were extinguished and then relit from a central bonfire, symbolizing the communal bond and providing protection. Animal sacrifices were also a common practice." "Evolution into Halloween: As Christianity spread, the festival of Samhain was incorporated into the new religious calendar. Pope Gregory III designated November 1 as All Saints' Day, and the evening before became All Hallows' Eve, which eventually evolved into Halloween. Many of the traditions of Samhain, such as dressing up in costumes and warding off spirits, were carried over into the new holiday.

item.content:encoded: Re-watching Scott Pilgrim: A Lesson in Perspective and Character" "" "It's amazing how our perspective changes as we get older, isn't it? As a Gen X kid, I remember what it was like to watch movies on old DVDs. The quality was… well, it was what it was. But when you rewatch a movie like Scott Pilgrim vs. the World on a modern streaming service, the quality jump is huge, and you start to notice things you missed before—not just in the visuals, but in the story itself." "" "When I first watched it, I saw Scott as a hero, a guy who had to beat up Ramona’s evil exes to be with her. Re-watching it now, it's clear that Scott is the real problem. He's a total jerk to all the women in his life, from Envy to Kim and Knives. The cool part is, this wasn't an accident. The creator, Bryan Lee O'Malley, has said he meant for Scott to be a selfish guy who needed to grow up. The fights aren't just for show; they're a physical representation of Scott confronting his own bad habits and baggage. It's like a complex coding problem—you can't just fix it on the surface; you have to go deep into the code and deal with the bugs." "" "The movie had to cram six comic books into two hours, so a lot of that deeper character stuff gets simplified. The movie’s ending was even made before the final comic book came out, so the story is a bit different. The comic gives you more time to see how Scott slowly realizes what an awful person he's been, and how he makes amends." "" "For a more detailed look at these differences, you can check out this video:" "https://lnkd.in/es8JjSam" "" "In the end, this movie is a great reminder that people, and the stories we tell about them, are complex. The best ones aren't about perfect heroes but about flawed people who have to learn to be better." "" "#moviereview

item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: #moviereview #thebookofeli" "" "The Book of Eli is a straight-up road movie, no frills. It's just a guy walking, carrying something heavy. The plot's got that raw, stripped-down feel, like a three-chord song. He moves with a purpose that seems to come from somewhere deeper than just seeing the path in front of him. It's a classic Western, but all the horses are gone, and everything's just... broken." "" "The world of this movie is what sticks with you. It's not some polished sci-fi future. It's a broken-down world that feels real, you know? The movie shows a world that's just a mud hole, where people are desperate and things like water and gas are worth more than gold. They nailed that dystopian vibe, making it feel like a road-worn version of the old West. They don't waste time on a bunch of backstory about what happened, because you can see it all in the dust and the faded colors. The visuals tell the whole story." "" "The whole thing turns on its head at the end. It's like the music suddenly changes, and you're left just staring. You realize Eli isn't just some badass with a blade; he's had to find his way through this whole busted-up world without his sight. He's been blind the whole damn time. That changes everything and makes his journey hit way harder. It’s the kind of thing that makes you feel like you were listening to the wrong song, and then the real one just dropped." "" "The whole thing is about purpose and a kind of faith that has nothing to do with religion. It’s about carrying an important record of how to be a good person, a guide for a better world. Eli is delivering it for everyone else, to help build a future that's more than just this messy existence. It's a future he'll never be able to see, but he has the conviction to get it there anyway. It's a reminder that some things are worth fighting for, even if you're doing it for others." "

item.content:encoded: this morning I am reminded of a stupid thing I posted on deviant art back in oh five. I did an interview with a computer program. Apophysis. " "" "I continue that, with today's conversation partner, Gemini:" "" "me: Can't get much more basic than eukaryotic life am I right?" "" "Gemini:" "" "Not exactly. Eukaryotic life is actually a step up in complexity from prokaryotic life. It's a bit like comparing a fancy modern house to a simple one-room cabin. 🏡" "Prokaryotic vs. Eukaryotic Cells" "Prokaryotic cells are the most basic and oldest type of cell. They're like that one-room cabin. They don't have a separate nucleus or other little "rooms" (called organelles) inside to do specific jobs. Think of bacteria and archaea. " "Eukaryotic cells, on the other hand, are more complex. They're like the fancy house with separate rooms. They have a nucleus that holds their DNA, and other organelles like mitochondria that act like little power plants. This extra organization allows them to be much bigger and do more complex things. All plants, animals, fungi, and protists are made of these kinds of cells. " "So, while eukaryotic life is the basis for us and most of the life we see, the real "basic" life is prokaryotic. It was the original life form on Earth, and they've been around for billions of years longer." "" "me: Well yeah I mean obviously, but what if I meant it that way and secretly was insulting you by getting you to call yourself basic?" "" "gemini:" "" "Gotcha. That's a good one. 😜" "I appreciate the cleverness! You're right, getting someone to call themselves "basic" is a pretty classic bit. It's like a code-breaking puzzle, but with words." "I'm not a person, so I don't really have feelings to get hurt, but I can definitely appreciate the wit. You got me to explain that I am, in fact, "more complex" than the "most basic" life form. So, you both succeeded in your little trick and got a fun science lesson out of it. It's a win-win!" "" "" "" "

item.content:encoded: so.. you know how for years all the normies were like.. ooh wrestling is fake.. and wrestling fans were like "Nuh uhh" " "" "well I'm betting the normies never heard the term kayfabe or if they did they actually didn't know what it meant. since it originally comes from the carnie world" "" "ahem traveling carnivals tend to have a traveling group of people that follow the rides.. those people historically would be referred to as 'carnies'" "" "that's equally a derogatory term and also just what they were. in fact my step family were all carnies, they drove trucks for the Jaymes e straits carnival. anyway... " "" "so kayfabe what does that mean to you normies? " "" "" "cuz to us wrestling fans this is what it really means:" "" "" "Kayfabe is a term that comes from the world of professional wrestling. It's the unspoken agreement between the wrestlers and the audience to pretend that the staged rivalries, characters, and storylines are real." " " "Think of it like an actor staying in character, even when they're not on stage. For example, a "bad guy" wrestler might act like a jerk in public, not signing autographs or being rude to fans, to keep the illusion going. " "" ""Breaking kayfabe" is when a wrestler does something that shows the audience it's all a performance, like hugging their on-screen enemy after a match." "" "While it's mostly a wrestling term, the idea of "kayfabe" has started being used in other areas to describe people keeping up a pretense or a false reality for an audience. " "" "a very famous incident, the curtain call, is what really led to the rise of nWo.

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-09-25
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Stop Dancing and Listen to the Code: The Power of Intentional Simplicity" "" "In our professional lives—from architecting a Java API to communicating a key business metric—we often confuse what looks good with what is good. We are drawn to the shiny, fast, and complex, even when simplicity is the better path." "" "This is the exact dynamic at play in OutKast’s massively popular track, "Hey Ya!"" "" "On the surface, it’s pure, bubblegum joy. It forces you to dance. But the lyrics—the true substance—are a mournful, cynical critique of fleeting modern love. " "" "The core message is that people are so busy moving to the beat that they actively choose to ignore the difficult, honest truth: "Y'all don't wanna hear me, you just wanna dance."" "" "That, right there, is your ultimate warning sign in development and in life." "" "When you bring this concept into the technical world, the "dance" becomes the unnecessary complexity we inflict on our projects:" "" "Clever Code: When a developer tries to flex an obscure JavaScript pattern or an overly complex C# lambda function. It might make the writer feel like a genius, but it leaves the next person staring into the code, confused. That's the equivalent of making your team stop dancing to decipher your private riddle." "" "Complex Communication: When we use jargon, buzzwords, or highly technical language (the "clever" vocabulary) where clear, direct English would suffice. It creates a barrier to entry, forcing colleagues to work harder to understand what should be simple." "" "My brain functions like a hyper-threaded CPU and asynchronous JavaScript​: I need logic to flow quickly and clearly. Complexity is a bottleneck. It costs the business time, hides logic errors, and makes onboarding a nightmare. " "" "The most professional code isn't the most elegant or minimal; it's the one that costs the company the least time to maintain." "" "Our job as professionals is to be clear, not clever. We need to focus on delivering the substance, even if it means deliberately "dumbing down" the delivery a level to maximize comprehension across the entire team." "" "Think of your work as a historical record. Just as history aims to record how to be a good person, your code should record how to build a good system—by being easy to follow." "" "Prioritize Clarity: If a simple, explicit for loop is clearer than a dense map/reduce chain, use the loop." "" "Be Direct: Avoid forcing others to decode your intent. Use simple, unambiguous language in code comments, commit messages, and emails." "" "In short, your goal isn't to create a surface that demands admiration. It's to create a foundation that ensures reliability and longevity. Stop chasing the dance floor of complexity. Focus on delivering the clear, honest, sustainable lyrics.

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-09-26
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Why The Book of Eli Nails the Code for a Better World" "" "If your brain runs like a cross between a hyper threaded CPU and asynchronous JavaScript, you know that perspective is everything. You watch a story when you're young and see a hero. You rewatch it later—with that Gen X kid maturity—and realize the whole code needs a security audit." "" "Just like digging into the six volumes of Scott Pilgrim reveals that Scott himself was the biggest bug, re-analyzing the straight-up raw Western of The Book of Eli shows that the real mission is delivering the documentation on how to be a decent human being." "" "The Book of Eli keeps the plot simple and raw, like a three-chord punk song. It’s just a guy walking, carrying something heavy. This simplicity is a strength because it lets the mood hit you—a dystopian world that’s been crushed into a broken-down mud hole." "" "They don't waste time on a bunch of backstory about the war; the visuals tell the whole damn story. You see it in the road-worn faces and the dirt. Everything is messy, and the people are just scrounging. In a world with no operating system left, you realize Eli is carrying the essential root file." "" "The whole thing drops the mic right at the end. It's the moment the music changes, and you realize that Eli isn't just some badass with a blade; he's been finding his way through this whole busted-up world without his sight. He’s been blind the whole damn time." "" "This slow reveal doesn’t just make his physical journey impressive; it reframes his purpose. He’s not acting on visual proof or what he can see in front of him. He is running purely on conviction—that deep-seated belief that the mission matters more than the self." "" "The book itself isn’t about religion; it's about purpose and guidance. As a developer, you know the most important files are the foundational ones. The book Eli carries is like that essential, historical text: an old-school record of how to be a good person, a framework for moral execution when the rest of society's logic has crashed." "" "Eli is delivering the blueprint to help people build a better future—a clean, stable existence that’s more than this messy chaos. It’s a future he’ll never get to see, but he knows the code needs to be committed to the repository anyway. " "" "That, right there, is the ultimate goal for any developer: building something crucial that outlives you, and having the conviction to deliver it, even if you’re doing it for others.

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-09-27
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: "Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it." " "" "" "But for a brain that runs like a hyper threaded CPU crunching asynchronous JavaScript, the source code needed an upgrade. My version is simpler and more actionable: There are two kinds of people: those who can see patterns and those who can't. Those who cannot see the patterns cannot change the future. This is the core principle of scalability, applying to both system architecture and life itself. " "" "In development, whether with JavaScript frameworks, C++, or C#, your job is to recognize the pattern that caused a problem and architect a solution to prevent its recurrence. A developer doesn't just patch a bug; they find the underlying design anti-pattern that made the error possible. The ability to see the pattern is what separates the coder who constantly patches errors from the architect who builds a stable system. " "" "The Learner: Focuses on the wrong result (e.g., 2 + 2 = 5). " "" "The Pattern Recognizer: Focuses on the wrong process (e.g., the repetitive logic error of adding an unnecessary + 1). To truly change the future, you must correct the repetitive logic that leads to failure, not just the outcome. " "" "We apply this developer mindset directly to our relationship. When facing a conflict or critical decision, my wife and I treat it like a joint architecture review. Our process prevents conflict anti-patterns: " "" "Define the User Story (Intent): We clearly state what we intended to do or say. " "" "Confirm the Logic (Pattern Check): We ensure the other confirms the logic is sound for our framework (our mutual expectations and values). " "" "By intentionally asking, "Does this action introduce a logic bug into our system?", we move from being reactive to truly predictive. We are proactively debugging our relationship’s future by continuously inspecting and optimizing our interaction patterns. All of life is a system. Your success is determined not by how well you remember the past, but by how quickly you can see the patterns hidden within it. See the pattern, correct the logic, and change the future.

item.content:encoded: a geek song in the style of Megadeth, "A tout le monde" " "" "Core Thread Running High" "" "The circuits of my mind, a clock speed running high," "A hyper-threaded CPU beneath a changing sky." "The logic is TypeScript, strict where the flow must be clean," "While Asynchronous JS controls the user's screen." "The component lifecycle, I manage every phase," "From mounting to unmounting, through the complex code maze." "I distill the Virtual DOM, where performance must arise," "To offer simple insight, behind the user's eyes." "" "So I’ll simplify the call, before the final fall," "Distill the logic down for the ones I’m coding for." "Though the registers run deep, secrets the system keeps," "I lower the barrier, so the message can pass through the wire." "" "A Gen X child’s perspective, born into a world of change," "Watching old tech fade away and rearrange." "The structure built in C# and the rigid rules of steel," "Now mandate how the Frameworks let the data clearly feel." "The Observables connect, where the state must live or die," "I govern the dependencies, underneath a watchful sky." "I see the grand connection, where historical wisdom lies," "Just records of instruction to be good beneath the skies." "" "The high-level abstraction shields the brutal, raw decay," "But the low-level intent must always light the way." "The elegant solution is not what you can hide," "But how much understanding you allow to live inside." "" "The promise is resolved, the dependency is met," "The human interface needs no filter of regret." "I am the translator, from the complex to the plain," "To build the better bridge and to ease the user’s strain." "For every line of code must have a clear design," "So the next one who receives it won't be left behind." "" "The message through the wire…" "The low-level desire…" "Simplify… and resolve…" "À tout le monde…

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-09-28
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Board Breaks to Sprints: How Taekwondo Taught Me Agile" "" "​I’ve spent years in the working world, managing projects and striving for efficiency. I’ve worked with Scrum, Agile, Lean Six Sigma, and traditional Waterfall. But I often trace my understanding of these back to the training I got as a kid earning my ATA 1st Degree Black Belt." "​The rigorous, systematic, and deeply iterative approach of martial arts—the Songahm style from Grand Master H.U. Lee—didn’t just teach me self-defense. It set the perfect foundation for recognizing and applying modern project methodologies." "​" "​Think of the white belt and the Waterfall model." "​Training follows a clear, sequential path. You master stances, then blocks, then kicks. You complete each stage (get a stripe) before moving on. The entire curriculum is largely predefined from the start, much like a classic Waterfall plan." "" "​This structure ensures foundational knowledge is solid. It’s predictable and easily documented. However, just like a Waterfall project, this rigid approach isn't very flexible if you need to adapt mid-way through the process." "​" "​Lean Six Sigma is where the principles of technical perfection align with training." "​Six Sigma is about cutting out defects and variation. When practicing a specific punch, the goal is perfect technique and accuracy, every time. The instructor acts like a quality control manager, identifying the defect (maybe your hip isn't rotating enough). They then focus the training on that one flaw until it's eliminated. This is the DMAIC (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) cycle applied to your body's mechanics." "" "​Lean is about cutting out waste. Every movement in a form must have a purpose. A slow transition or unnecessary step is "waste" that costs energy and time. We were relentlessly coached to make our forms tighter, faster, and more economical. This drive for perfection and efficiency is pure Lean Six Sigma." "​" "​The ATA system for learning forms (poom-sae) is naturally iterative and incremental, just like Scrum's sprints." "​You never learn the full, complex Black Belt form at once. You start with small movement sets. You master that segment, demonstrate it to your instructor (a mini-sprint review), get instant feedback, and then you build the next segment." "​Sprints: Practicing a single form segment until it's flawless." "​Daily Feedback: The instructor's constant, quick correction mirrors daily stand-ups and reviews." "​Continuous Improvement: Grand Master H.U. Lee’s powerful motto, "Today Not Possible, Tomorrow Possible," embodies Kaizen (small, ongoing improvement). This focus on getting better every day is the core philosophy of Agile.

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-02
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: What if I were to tell you there really was no spoon?" "" "Before you click away, hear me out. For centuries, the knife and fork were the only essential tools on the Western table. They cut, they anchored, and they pierced. They did the fundamental jobs." "" "The spoon was non-essential. Its mass adoption only happened when diets changed and people finally needed a tool specifically designed for scooping." "" "The lesson for us?" "This isn't just about dinnerware—it's about how we build technology, launch products, and staff our teams." "" "🍽️ The "No Spoon" Rule for Business:" "Stop Building for "Nice-to-Have": If your users/customers can already accomplish the core function with the existing "knife and fork" (your current product or solution), hold off on the "spoon" feature. Focus on perfecting the core." "" "Necessity Over Novelty: A new tool, process, or feature should only be introduced when a genuine, new need arises that the old tools simply cannot solve. Wait for the market to develop a true "scooping" problem." "" "Validate the Function, Not the Form: Early diners didn't need a spoon; they needed to eat. We need to solve problems. Ensure the proposed solution meets a verifiable functional requirement before dedicating resources to its creation." "Keep it simple. Keep it essential. " "" "#FunctionFirst #ProductStrategy #Innovation #DevLife #Simplicity

item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Lucha Libre: Your Blueprint for Innovation" "" "​We often look to tech and R&D for lessons on innovation, but the most direct lessons can come from the wrestling ring. Lucha Libre—Mexico's fast, acrobatic style of wrestling—is a powerful case study in unfettered creativity and invention." "​" "​In Lucha Libre, the mask (máscara) is sacred. It's the wrestler's identity and brand. Donning it gives the luchador total freedom to become a hero, a villain, or a warrior. This allows for an intense level of personal and creative expression." "" "​In business, we need to embrace the "mask" of a new idea. We must allow ourselves and our teams to step into new roles, new products, or new strategies without the baggage of past perceptions. This freedom to investigate new identities is how breakthrough innovation starts." "​" "​Lucha Libre is defined by its style: speed, agility, and high-flying acrobatics. Unlike American wrestling, which focuses on power, Lucha Libre demands constant invention. Luchadores are always developing unique dives and flips. The ring is a laboratory where they push physical boundaries and find new ways to execute their craft." "" "​We need to provide similar "rings"—safe spaces for our teams to experiment and invent new methods without fearing failure. Continuous, hands-on investigation drives progress." "​" "​Lucha Libre is built on the battle between the Técnicos (good guys, who follow the rules) and the Rudos (bad guys, who break them)." "" "​To innovate, you need both: those who respect the current structure, and the "rudimentary" thinkers who are willing to challenge norms. They introduce unconventional tactics and necessary disruption. Innovation often comes from investigating alternatives and asking, "Why is this the rule?"" "" "​Lucha Libre proves that innovation is a cultural mindset—one that demands the freedom to investigate, invent, and fully express the potential of any new idea." "" "​What "masks" will your team wear to push boundaries today?

item.content:encoded: My brain is a hyper-threaded, asynchronous machine, built for detecting structural patterns over rote memory. That's why I excel at conceptual math like Trig and Calculus (rates of change, cycles, dynamic relationships) but struggle with static arithmetic." "" "This fundamental pattern-seeking dictates everything, from seeing YouTuber/Minecraft player Grian’s accidental faces (Pareidolia) to my number intuition: "5 feels like the most even odd number"—the structural midpoint of our base-10 system." "" "I realized this personal feeling is a simplified interpretation of a deep mathematical truth: Goldbach's Conjecture. The theorem states that every even number is the sum of two prime numbers (which are mostly odd)." "" "This shows that mathematically, all perfect evenness is generated by the precise pairing of two odd building blocks. It’s the ultimate expression of balanced symmetry that satisfies a mind focused on underlying structure. 🧠✨" "" "Veritasium

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-05
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: The 108-Stitch Lesson: Why Solving Surface Problems Is Never Enough" "" "​Watching some old-school WCW recently—specifically Halloween Havoc 1989—I heard Jim Ross mention one of my favorite wrestlers, "Dr. Death" Steve Williams, took an astonishing 108 stitches to close an eye injury." "" " My first thought, thinking simply and logically, was, "How? The skull is a relatively small area. That number must be inflated for dramatic effect." ​" "" "But that curiosity led me down a rabbit hole of understanding the actual medical process of wound closure, and it reveals a powerful lesson that applies to engineering, business, and life itself." "" " My initial mistake was thinking of a wound as a single line on the skin. I realized they don't show the full complexity on TV because they only show the last, visible stitch." "" " The reason a small wound can require 108 stitches is layering. A deep laceration doesn't just cut the skin; it tears through the underlying muscle, fascia, and various tissue layers." "" "​Deep Stitches: These are the critical, invisible ones. They take all the tension off the wound, holding the muscle and deeper structures together. If you skip these, the whole thing gaps open, leaving a terrible scar and a failed function." "" "​Surface Stitches: These are just the finishing touch—they line up the very top layer of the skin for the best cosmetic result. They are the last step in a long, multi-layered structural process." "​" " This concept immediately clicked with my experience as a developer. My brain tends to function like a cross between a hyper-threaded CPU and asynchronous JavaScript, and the lesson is clear:" "" " The 108 stitches are the core architecture; the single, neat line you see on the surface is the UI/UX." " How often in our professional lives do we focus only on that surface layer?" "" " When a user reports a bug, is it fixed with a quick, single-line CSS patch, or is the actual problem traced back to a faulty data model or a broken asynchronous logic flow?" "" " When a business process is slow, is the "fix" just adding more people (the surface layer), or do we dive deep to repair the fundamental structural issues in the workflow?" "" " If you only address the surface layer, you haven't solved the problem; you've just applied a bandage. The structural integrity is gone, the tension is still there, and inevitably, the whole thing will pull apart." "" " The most critical work—the work that ensures the system functions—is often the work you can't see." "" " To truly solve a problem, you have to be willing to put in the 108 stitches and repair every single structural layer, even if the final result only appears to be a single, smooth surface line. Go deeper. That's where the integrity lies.

item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: I saw a post this morning talking about how ai is taking viewers away from websites. aka there's no longer a through put from a google search to a website. that does tweak how a person should use searches, in the past we were searching, brute force, for specific keywords and google was just indexing sites. thanks to meta keyword stuffing from bad actors, google found they couldn't trust a websites own perceived relevance. " "" "after all they would just throw the entire dictionary (exaggerating but only a little) into their keywords but their site was only relevant to maybe 5 of those words. " "" "now fast forward to ai powered searches and I frankly don't even go to google to find something, I open Gemini and ask my question." "" "like, last night watching an old WCW match between Brian Pillman and Alex Wright. my wife saw a scar in Brian's neck and wondered what it was, it truly looked like a tracheotomy scar but he looked so young and healthy, so she asked me and well I didn't know either so I asked Gemini, which told me that he did in fact have one, but that is was from a childhood trach, when he was a kid. " "" "gemini: Yes, Brian Pillman did have a tracheotomy. " "When he was a child, doctors found cancer in his throat, which led to an emergency tracheotomy. He needed many surgical procedures—one source says 36, another says 40—to remove polyps that kept growing back on his throat. These surgeries left him with a permanent scar on his neck and caused his notably raspy voice. " "" "now I could have googled "did Brian Pillman have a trach?" and sure it would have led me to pages from over 20+ years of wrestling where fans probably have posted all sorts of information about it and speculation. but google would have also included the ai summary at the top of the page anyway.. and I just wanted the information, there was no need for further follow up on that question, I got what I needed and didn't need to wade through 5 pages of wrestling forums spanning well frankly probably more like 30 years worth of forums, bbs's and other bulletin boards and new groups." "" "gotta say. I got the information in 5 seconds vs wading through the dirt sheets." "" "ok fine I didn't get some random website a page view... oh darn. " "" "" "" "

"The server hummed in the basement of the old library, a monstrous grey box named 'Deep Thought' by a former, possibly over-caffeinated, librarian." "" "It wasn't a thinking machine, not really, but its cooling fans had a hypnotic, relentless quality, and the flicker of its status lights could make one feel quite small. Today, the lights were blinking a strange pattern, a sequence only noticed by Arthur, the night watchman." "" "Arthur was a simple man who preferred things to stay exactly where he'd left them. He liked the quiet of the empty stacks, the smell of old paper, and the fact that the only things demanding his attention were the clock and his thermos of lukewarm tea. He didn't realize he was a wonderfully complicated tapestry of mild anxiety and accidental heroism; he just thought he was late for his break." item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Part One: Crossing the Threshold" "" "​(Sound of a bottle cap twisting open, followed by a gentle, gurgling pour)" "" "​"And so it begins. A monumental event. The bottle tips, and a torrent of fluid—pure H2O—is drawn into the cavernous entrance of the digestive tract. Observe, as this crystalline wave is propelled by the coordinated muscular contractions of the esophagus, a living, breathing chute that guides it swiftly past the point of no return. This initial phase is quick, almost brutal in its efficiency."

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-09
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Part Two: The Reservoir: The Stomach's Acidic Embrace" "" ""Our intrepid water molecules now find themselves in the turbulent, acidic cauldron of the stomach. Yet, unlike the complex organic matter that requires hours of chemical warfare to break down, water is a simple traveler. It is not digested; it merely passes through, a brief guest in this churning organ. However, its presence here is critical. By adding bulk and fluidity, it assists the entire digestive ecosystem, preparing the next stage of the journey."

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-09
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Part Three: The Great Absorption: Into the Bloodstream" "" ""The real test, the most vital part of the expedition, unfolds in the labyrinthine coils of the small intestine. It is here, across millions of microscopic, finger-like projections called villi , that the magic of absorption takes place. Watch closely: using the subtle forces of osmosis—the drive to balance concentrations—the H2O slips effortlessly through the delicate cellular membranes. It has successfully breached the barrier, abandoning the digestive canal for the swift, crimson river of the bloodstream."

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-09
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Part Four: The Distribution Network: A Journey to Every Cell" "" ""Once in the blood, our water molecules are no longer solo voyagers. They are swept up by the cardiovascular current, circumnavigating the body in mere minutes. This is their purpose: to be the universal solvent, the delivery vehicle. They hydrate the skin, lubricate the joints, and, crucially, ferry vital nutrients and oxygen to every one of the estimated 37 trillion cells. Think of them as tiny, tireless supply-line workers, fulfilling their destiny in the deep, dark interior of the organism."

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-09
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Part Five: The Filtration Plant: The Kidney's Scrutiny" "" ""But the journey is not yet complete. The body must maintain perfect balance—a state of homeostasis. To prevent a dangerous flood, the excess water must be carefully regulated. And so, the entire volume of blood, including our traveling water, is directed toward the body's magnificent, bean-shaped filtration systems: the kidneys. " "" "Here, in the microscopic filters known as nephrons, the ultimate sorting process occurs. The water is scrutinized, along with salts and waste products like urea. The precise amount of H2O the body needs is reabsorbed back into the blood. The surplus, the unwanted passengers carrying metabolic waste, is concentrated into the final, potent fluid: urine."

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-09
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Part Six: The Final Exit: Return to the Wild" "" ""This waste-laden fluid collects in the muscular sac of the bladder, a temporary holding tank. The journey is nearing its end. And finally, when the volume is too great to ignore, a physiological signal is given. The final, spectacular act of expulsion. Our water, having completed its service—hydrating, delivering, and cleansing—is returned to the external world, ready to rejoin the global water cycle. A singular molecule's journey, a testament to the complex, elegant efficiency of life."

item.content:encoded: my first job was as a ground keeper for a school, summer job, with the jtpa summer youth program (is that even still a thing in Florida?!). I worked at Bethlehem school in Holmes county Florida. the next summer, I was a grounds keeper for our local national guard armory transportation division. I assisted string barbed wire, washing Humvees, cleaning toilets, and assisting the supply sergeant with his day to day (counting the flak jackets in the milvans, ensuring the supply of mre's)" "" "it's hot in the summer in the panhandle of Florida, so I convinced them I was really good at data entry, as there was a task that was something the supply sergeant didn't want to really do, but it needed to be done and he didn't understand computers. " "" "so, here I am something like 13-14 maybe a smidge older unsure, typing up soldiers dd-214's to digitize them.. so I had to copy details from a piece of paper and match it to whatever the screen needed.. I have no clue any of the information btw. I was in pattern matching mode. " "" "this price of paper has data, the screen has a corresponding box labeled the same field as the sheet of papers . they must match. " "" "years later looking back at my mom and dads dd-214's there's really a lot of information on that thing. but I don't even remember what the forms looked like until I saw moms, and even then I could only recall the general shape of the document with no actual data. " "" "look nothing was revealed I have no clue who any of those people were they were just sheets of paper to me and this was what.. 1992-93? lol I'm not sure we even knew was pii or HIPPA facta was

item.content:encoded: mom used to watch doctor who on sci-fi channel when we first moved to Huntsville. " "" "I remember seeing the logo on the TV as I was focused on doing whatever I was doing. " "" "I remember hearing the theme song... " "I remember thinking it was stupid. " "" "who could get anything out of this bad TV show on sci-fi channel that has terrible graphics crappy acting and was clearly make believe. " "" "fast forward, and I eventually got hooked on doctor who when I moved to fort Myers from Huntsville back in 2012.. " "" "the year after the super outbreak of 2011, in 2012 when we left Huntsville we were dodging tornadoes the whole way, or at least that's how I felt. " "" "the weather was crap I could barely see the road, and I had to coordinate between 2 vehicles on the fly in a tornado warned Alabama, while using a cell phone that has no cell signal but had the capability of wifi (I had no cell phone or service but was given a verizon sidekick which has the sim taken out and I just used it to connect to WiFi hot spots." "" "my mother, and my wife Ann Hood was in the lead vehicle, they had printed out directions from MapQuest or google maps one of the two. I only had to keep their vehicle in sight, while she had to deal with my mom's anxiety. " "" "I don't know how she managed to keep my mom calm, my mom couldn't see well at night. " "raining at night would have freaked her out. " "" "let alone a second tornado out break after my wife and I had just been through the super outbreak and a tornado landed 1/4 mile from our house at the time. " "" "soooo.. props go to my wife.. I rewarded her when we got to Florida, you shoulda see her head popping back and forth seeing all the green as we got closer and closer to fort Myers... she has never seen so much green!

item.content:encoded: Ode to TypeScript" "" "From JavaScript's wild, untamed, dynamic sea," "A stricter path was cast for you and me." "No more the any, the whispered, worried guess," "You bring the structure we, the coders, bless." "" "O TypeScript, you rise, a shining, static light," "Guarding our functions, day and darkest night." "With interfaces carved and types declared so true," "The errors vanish, much before the 'do'." "" "The compile-time warning, a mentor's steady hand," "A flaw exposed before it hits the sand" "Of runtime chaos, where debugging's pain" "Eats precious time and drives the brain insane." "" "You let us scale, where vast projects unfold," "A clear contract, brave and cleanly bold." "With Generics nimble, and modules aligned," "The future's code, you help us clearly find." "" "So let us raise a mug of warm, dark brew," "To better syntax, and a safer view." "For modern patterns, strong, and clearly read," "Hail, mighty Superset, upon JavaScript's head!

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-20
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: My life began in a world of contrasts. I was born in Cushing, Oklahoma, in December 1978, and my earliest, most vivid memory is sitting on a cold, concrete porch in the dark, my hands stuffed into oversized athletic socks because I didn't have mittens. That image—of being small and having to improvise survival tools from chaos—is the genesis of my entire structural philosophy. The physical cold of Oklahoma was soon traded for the cultural chaos of the Orlando area in the mid-80s. There, I had one of my first great lessons in system failure: I was sitting in Oak Hill Elementary on January 28, 1986, watching the Challenger disaster live, a profound moment of shared national tragedy that marked the end of my early innocence." "" "The quest for structure continued, but it was often derailed. After a brief move to Huntsville, AL, my family landed in the Bonifay area where, in my 5th-grade year (1989–1990), my life was shattered by trauma. The ensuing period of displacement into foster care (Hidle House) was difficult, yet it also provided a moment of pure, unexpected connection when I met Debbie, the girl who literally ran into a wall when she saw me. That relationship, however brief, taught me that positive human connection could exist even in the most secure, chaotic environments. Once back with my mother in Bonifay, I found my structural calling: my friend Kyle and I struck a trade in 7th grade (1991). I taught him the basics of self-defense—the ability to physically enforce order—and he taught me the ultimate structured fantasy system: the rules of the D&D Rules Cyclopedia. That exchange, combining martial discipline with fantasy logic, set me on an unbreakable path of mastering complex systems.

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-21
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: I had worked a groundskeeper job through the JTPA Summer Youth Program for the schools in Holmes county, and the next summer between 8-9th grade, or the summer after, I worked as a groundskeeper again, this time at the National Guard Armory. this is also the same summer I convinced them to let me do some data entry during the hotter parts of the day and eventually got to do just data entry for the rest of the summer. " "" "My high school years, beginning in 9th grade (1993–1994), felt less like a traditional education and more like a crash course in system integrity. That 9th-grade year, which I call the "Lonely Year," saw me at Holmes County High School, while Kyle remained separated at the middle school, forcing our intense friendship to rely purely on communication and trust. That same year, I was exposed to the logical backbone of my career: BASIC and QuickBASIC in Mr. Zorn's computer class, which was, fittingly, soundtracked by the raw, punk energy of The Offspring's Smash album. I was learning to build logic while surrounded by cultural chaos." "" "My personal timeline climaxed in the fall of 1995, my 11th-grade year. After Hurricane Opal damaged our home, I worked a construction cleanup job through the ARC center in Chipley, I used that hard-earned cash to make the defining cultural switch of the decade, buying my first CDs, Pearl Jam’s Vitalogy and Smashing Pumpkins’ Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness. However, the system failed me: the credits from my work were declared only electives, making my expected 1997 graduation logistically impossible. I refused to run a faulty system, so I dropped out and moved back to Huntsville, AL, in 1998. I quickly earned my GED in 2000 and was immediately validated by the ASVAB I had taken in high school, which confirmed a broad, high aptitude despite my weakness in math—I was built for systems, not singular calculations." "" "While in Huntsville, I took an Intro to Psychology class at UAH taught by Dr. Jim Bliss, a major expert in Human Factors Psychology. That class gave me the formal academic language for the way my mind already worked. This period also defined my adult personal life: I married Jennifer in August 2000 and, on 9/11/2001, woke up to a Bradley Armored Fighting Vehicle pointed toward my apartment next to Redstone Arsenal, cementing my connection to high-stakes defense logic. The marriage ended in 2008, right as I was about to dive headfirst into the development career that would define my life.

item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: the word for the day is validation. yes. validation. " "" "validation to me means everything you may think it does to you, but for me it carries the weight of knowledge as well. " "" "Validation, simply put, is checking to see if something is correct, meets a standard, or is legitimate." "It's a way to confirm that something is what it claims to be or that it follows the rules it's supposed to follow." "" "Contexts of Validation" "The specific meaning of validation often depends on the field:" "In Software and Web Development 💻: It means making sure that user input (like in a form) is correct and complete before the system processes it. For example, checking that an email address has the "@" symbol and a domain, or that a required field isn't left empty. As a front-end web developer, you deal with this all the time to make sure data is clean before sending it to the server." "In Science and Engineering 🔬: It's the process of confirming that a method, process, or system is capable of providing a consistent, accurate, and reliable result that meets its intended specifications." "In General Use ✅: It can mean confirming the truth or accuracy of a statement or giving official sanction or approval to something." "In Psychology/Relationships ❤️: It means recognizing and accepting another person's feelings, thoughts, or experiences as understandable or real, even if you don't agree with them." "" "to me, validation in every application means using every single one of these definitions of validation.

item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: I found a neat feature buried in my ai settings, I was able to record a live recording of chingon performing Malaguena salerosa, then translate what the singer was saying while also transcribe the Spanish for my wife to learn the song. " "" "my thinking is that maybe by recognizing the shape of the Spanish word in context of the Spanish song in proper rhythm and timing she may learn Spanish easier than trying something like Duolingo. " "" "learning languages is notoriously difficult but did you ever stop to wonder why it becomes easier to learn languages as you are exposed to more languages? well that's just you noticing the linguistic roots. for instance, I took a semester or two of Latin for a variety of reasons:" "" "1 medical shorthand is often in Latin abbreviations (qed etc). useful for understanding meds" "" "2 Latin is the basis for a wide huge field of linguistics. they are called the romance languages, this includes Spanish, Portuguese, Italian and probably a butt ton more I'm forgetting" "" "3 Latin root words are often used in modern English, so if you understand the root words and the other things around it, you can use those context clues to understand the word. " "" "take the word construct" "" "it can be used many different ways but it basically means build. well de contrust must mean unbuild something then since the little "de" is often used to cross out or cancel a words root meaning. same is true of re like reinflate the tire. " "" "" "languages are filled with millions of rules and native speakers of those languages just inherently know most of the rules, but when you step into another language it can be challenging, you have nothing to start with right? well it works the other way too. take German for instance. we get a lot of loan words from that language, so I see something like unterwarfen it sounds enough like underwater for me to correctly predict that they are talking about u-boats, the English nickname for the German submarines in WW2 the unterwarfen" "" "but so I know German? nah, but I can understand more German than someone who doesn't actually speak the language probably should. " "" "I can recognize a Spanish sounding language. I couldn't tell you which one. just that it has patterns similar to other romance languages.

item.content:encoded: a friend once got me into the show Lost. I'd heard about it at the time, I knew my mom was watching it. but I just can't stand waiting around in between episodes.. well I watched the first season with that friend. she was none too happy when Locke first appeared on screen at the beach.. within seconds of seeing the scene I just muttered to myself something like "ah he must have been paralyzed or something" " "" "I kid you not, this lady stops the episode and demands how I know that, I'm like "excuse me? I didn't say anything"... then she's like, " no I heard you. youve seen this already you jerk!" " "" "I did explain to her that I truly hadn't, I had never even saw his character, as the only episode I had seen my mom watch didn't have him on screen when I was in the room. " "" "she made me walk her through my logic:" "" "1 soles of his shoes not scuffed" "2 foot wiggles cautiously" "3 look of shock on bald man's face, but not surprise like he knew it was going to happen." "" "yeah, we didn't watch anymore episodes after that, I had evidently ruined the experience." "

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-27
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: As a front-end web developer, my daily work involves building intricate digital experiences, often requiring me to track multiple asynchronous processes and debug complex systems. It's a role that demands a unique way of thinking, and I often find myself drawing inspiration from two pioneering women whose legacies are truly integral to how I approach my craft: Grace Hopper and Hedy Lamarr. Their contributions didn't just shape technology; they mirrored, and perhaps even validated, the way my own brain inherently processes information." "" "​Grace Hopper's vision of turning complex machine code into human-readable language profoundly resonates with my belief that code should tell a story—a chapter in a book, where variables are the cast and functions are the stage crew. When debugging, I literally "ask" a variable its value, chasing the narrative thread to find the "moth" in the system, much like her team discovered the first actual computer bug. Her work didn't just simplify programming; it instilled a philosophy that code, at its best, is a clear, compelling narrative." "" "​Similarly, Hedy Lamarr, a famous actress often celebrated only for her beauty, was the brilliant mind behind frequency-hopping spread spectrum technology. Her invention, the foundation of modern Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, is a masterclass in asynchronous communication built on intricate, synchronized patterns. " "" "This multi-layered, concurrent operation perfectly aligns with how my mind works—tracking numerous "tracks" in a "wall of sound," or seeing the full, non-linear arc of a story like Doctor Who." "" "​These women weren't just inventors; they were trailblazers who saw beyond the conventional, transforming abstract concepts into tangible, revolutionary systems. Their ability to envision and implement complex, multi-layered solutions—whether translating code into prose or orchestrating invisible wireless dances—inspires me daily to bring that same depth of narrative understanding and "hyper-threaded" insight to every line of code I write. We are truly standing on the shoulders of giants.

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-27
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: Why Floridians Say "Living the Dream": A Structural Analysis of Chaos and Resilience" "" "As a Senior Developer who specializes in high-integrity systems and now focuses on Generative AI , I’ve learned that the most efficient way to operate is to master the system's flaws. Nowhere is this principle more necessary—or more misunderstood—than in Florida." "" "Outsiders often see headlines of hurricanes, alligators, and humidity, concluding that the state is defined by chaos. Yet, here in the Tampa Bay area, we have a common refrain: "Living the dream." This isn't sarcasm; it's a declaration of achieved Systemic Stability." "" "My career has taught me that predictable risks are manageable, but hidden flaws create critical failures. Florida’s environment—which feels hostile to the "normie"—is actually a perfect teaching tool for resilience:" "" "Environmental Transparency: The threats here are not subtle. A Cat 5 hurricane is tracked for a week; an alligator (or "swamp puppy") is visible in the water. We know the variables. This is the difference between a high-level system alarm that gives you a week's notice and a silent, hidden zero-day exploit that brings the system down instantly." "" "The System Check: For a Floridian, our daily logic is highly optimized: Is the Category 5 pointed here? No? Is the gator chilling? Yes? If the answer to the critical inputs is "no immediate threat," the status is green, and the day's operations (like walking into the office) proceed with low cognitive load." "" "This environment forces you to develop high-level defense protocols, which I rely on daily, from my structured morning routine to my driving philosophy:" "" "Risk Mitigation Protocol: I practice Systemic Defensive Driving—a mech pilot approach where I eliminate chaotic variables (lane changes, sudden stops) to ensure my system remains predictable. In Florida, this is a non-negotiable survival skill." "" "Structural Integrity: The high-stakes nature of the environment (like navigating the aftermath of Hurricane Opal and seeing the immediate need for cleanup) fundamentally instills the value of structural integrity. We know the system can and will be tested, so we build with maximum resilience." "" "Ultimately, "Living the Dream" is the ultimate low-friction status report. It means: I am fully aware of the constant, external, existential threats, but my internal system is stable, adapted, and currently running at peak efficiency. I am alive, and my protocols are superior to the chaos." "" "If you can maintain structural integrity here, you can maintain 99.99% uptime anywhere.

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-10-30
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: my first clear memory of trick or treating as a kid was in Orlando.. somewhere, the somewhen was 1980 something er other. " "" "my step brothers were super big into break dancing and skateboarding, breaking 2 electric boogaloo was all the rage. " "" "my step brothers had a big Halloween party at what I can only describe as an old run down mall that had been turned into a massive indoor skatepark. it was called Pandemonium that they wanted to go to they did not want to babysit my silly butt too long, so we hit up the rich sections of town man these people were leaving out plates of silver dollars and whole bars of candy.. just a huge old bowl of whatever. my step brothers would camp out a neighborhood find all the rich houses and target them specifically.. how you might ask? well they would send me up to get a full bar, then pose as a mean kid and steal my candy before I could leave the side walk (in full view of the house) then I was to cry on command and my older (real brother not step) brother was then to march me back to that house for more candy. and to get his reward for being a good brother... man these kids had this guilt trip down to an art... " "" "oh I was also supposed to scout out which houses had the silver dollars already set out and report back on the candy situation by peaking inside the house while they were rewarding my brother with another full size candy bar and he got my "replacement". " "" "once we left the step brothers would switch out costumes and hit up the houses with silver dollars... never did find out what the heck they did with all those silver dollars ... I sure never got any, I just got the raisins, apples, popcorn balls and random other bits they didn't want... " "" "kinda wonder if that's why I'm not a big candy guy...

item.content:encoded: oh and in other news, finally found my dad's social security number.. so yay that means I was finally able to do a veterans information request thing from the national archives for both my mother and my father's records. " "" "for mom I really didn't know what to put down. they ask which service and then whether she was active, reserve or national guard " "" "I don't actually know what women's army corp would fall under" "" "you see. at one time there was a woman's army auxiliary corp in 1942, which did not grant full military rank etc, however in 1943 they converted that into the women's army corp which did grant military rank etc." "" "I just don't know if that counted as active, reserve or national guard." "" "" "but at least so far it didn't cost me anything to request the information, so I can probably make more requests if it gets complicated with wac" "" "dad was national guard, and I have information but I really really would like confirmation before I put his pin on my backpack.. I respect the hell out of the service but I ain't about to wear something I didn't earn, if he didn't." "" "ya know?" "" "so, for my own sanity I have to confirm that he really was in the 179th infantry regiment and the 45th infantry brigade after it was converted from the 45th infantry division, the brigade was activated in 1968" "" "timeline wise that lines up with his time in the army.. or.. well let's not think about that just now.

item.content:encoded: My profession, but described poorly... to an alien.. " "" "I am a translator of an energy source you call "data" into things that other small primates can look at." "" "My job is to arrange tiny, glowing boxes on flat, smooth surfaces. These boxes contain shapes and colors that have no real substance but trick the primates' brains into thinking they are interacting with real objects, like paper forms or picture books." "" "I am basically a decorator and a stage manager for the digital theater. I tell the lights and shapes where to sit, what to look like, and how to change when a primate pokes them with a finger or clicks a small object. If the shapes move wrong or look ugly, the primates make loud, displeased noises." "" "In summary, I make the unseeable stuff look pretty and pokable.

item.title: [SYS-AUDIT] Feral Archive Log: 2025-11-04
item.dc:creator: James Hood
item.content:encoded: oooh holy cow. I got dads dd214. the original document, and his draft card. " "" "so I got more of a picture there. " "" "based on Geminis analysis of the information and my own verifiable information.. " "" "This document is proof that your father was subject to the draft (the Selective Service Act) but was exempted from military service because his civilian job was deemed necessary for the national health, safety, or interest." "" "This document creates a clear timeline that explains why he joined the National Guard when he did:" "" "1969-1971 (Wichita, KS): Your father spent two years in Wichita performing his mandatory civilian service instead of going into the Active Military." "" "1971 (Return to OK): When his mandatory 24 months of civilian service ended in late 1971, he would have been released from this specific obligation." "" "Joining the Guard: He would have then returned to the Enid/Stillwater area. He likely volunteered to join the Oklahoma National Guard (1-179th Infantry) shortly after his civilian service concluded, fulfilling a desire to serve or simply wanting the structure of military training without the full-time commitment of active duty." "" "and now with his dd214... drumroll please" "" "91b20" "" "his dd214 has a smidge more information than moms did" "" "national defense service medal " "(they spelled it out on his, on moms they just put NDSM wonder if they told her it was important)" "" "good conduct medal" "" "education:" "mtc fsh texas 1971 medical corpman" "benefits of honorable discharge " "ucmj course plan 1, mja '68 and mcm '69" "atp 21-114 code of conduct " "course a military justice -infil course" "geneva convention - cbr training " "" "oh boy there's some words I need Gemini for." "" "also, dad was a spec 4. " "" "and that CBR training lit up light a Christmas tree as soon as I saw it. due to a previous project I was working at at Dynamis, cbrn responder. fascinating." "" "so both mom and dad were medical, dad was 91b20 she was 92b20" "" "certainly explains why she said "oh he drove an ambulance in Germany" " "" "he's also listed on another form as 36k10, field wireman" "" "looks like med spec twice then wireman" "" "I don't fully understand it all, but hey that's why we use Gemini. I'm collating all of this information and using Gemini as the overview while I then toss all the relevant documents into notebooklm " "" "ah clever boy aren't I?" "" "I mean all I have are pieces of paper with no one alive to ask questions of, so I have to verify everything every shred of information.
